items.title: US$200m chicken import bill puts local poultry production in focus – Forson
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson has questioned Ghana’s annual spending of about US$200 million on chicken imports, arguing that local maize and soybean production could support a stronger domestic poultry industry. Speaking in an interview on Thursday after presenting the 2027 Budget to Parliament, he identified agricultural modernisation as essential to reducing food imports. “Why should we be importing about $200 million of chicken every year?” he asked. “Why, why can’t we use our land to grow soybean and maize to feed the poultry industry?” Dr Forson said Ghana’s land, water resources and youthful population offered a competitive advantage. However, he argued that the existing approach to agriculture could not meet the country’s needs. “The current agriculture, peasant agriculture, cannot solve the problems.” He put Ghana’s annual food import bill at about US$3.5 billion and questioned continued dependence on foreign supplies of products the country could produce. “We spend about 3.5 billion United States dollars yearly to bring foodstuffs into our country. It cannot continue.” His comments followed a question about planned spending on commercial agriculture and agribusiness, including poultry, maize, soybean, rice, oil palm, sugar, aquaculture and vegetables. The minister also raised concerns about fish imports and reliance on neighbouring Burkina Faso for onions and tomatoes. “We spend hundreds of millions of dollars every year to bring in vegetables. Pwalugu can be the solution.” Beyond food production, Dr Forson said the government wanted more of Ghana’s cocoa processed domestically. He argued that the longstanding model of buying beans and shipping them abroad allowed other countries to capture the benefits of value addition. “We are not saying don’t come and buy our cocoa beans, but if you are company out there, come and buy our cocoa beans, but add value here in Ghana.” Dr Forson said a new Cocoa Board Act provided for 50% local processing. He indicated that a legislative instrument would set out a timeline to reach 100% by 2030. Addressing questions about processing capacity, he disclosed discussions with Dangote over a proposed investment in Ghana. “Dangote has reached out to use Ghana as a hub to process cocoa locally.” He said the discussions concerned processing 500,000 metric tonnes of cocoa in Ghana. The parties were reviewing the terms of a proposed contract.

items.title: Joint investigation team seizes pistol of Mir Raza’s business partner
items.description: KARACHI: The Joint Investigation Team (JIT), formed by the Sindh government, to probe the mysterious death of a young businessman, Mir Raza Ali, has seized the licensed pistol of his partner. Without naming the partner, West DIG Irfan Baloch, who heads the JIT, said on Thursday that the North Nazimabad branch of Mir Raza’s food chain has also been sealed for further investigation. The JIT was formed on the recommendation of the judicial commission headed by a Sindh High Court judge to probe the alleged murder of Mir Raza. According to an official statement issued by the DIG Baloch: “The police have recovered the licensed pistol of the partner, took [control of] the food chain previously run by him and seized its record”. The seized weapon has been sent to the police’s forensic science lab for analysis. “The JIT is thoroughly examining all aspects of the case,” said the DIG. Further investigation of the case in the light of evidence and seized record is underway, according to the statement. Mir Raza, 25, had gone missing from his PECHS residence on July 28, 2026 and his body bearing a gunshot wound was found the next day in the bushes opposite University of Karachi’s main gate in Gulistan-i-Jauhar. The investigators during preliminary probe termed it a suicide case, a claim rejected by his family. The judicial commission led by Justice Omar Sial of the SHC, while severely criticising the police investigation, came to the conclusion that it was a ‘murder’, and made a host of recommendations, including formation of a JIT to probe the murder. Published in Dawn, November 13th, 2026

items.title: ESA’s Euclid telescope maps over 900 million galaxies
items.description: PARIS: The European Space Agency has released its first big collection of data from the orbiting Euclid telescope’s mission to map the universe’s large-scale structure, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies, as scientists investigate the puzzling cosmic components dark matter and dark energy. The data unveiled on Thursday covered a survey of the sky equal to about 9,500 times the size of the moon as viewed from Earth. The mission’s goal is to complete the largest-ever three-dimensional atlas of the cosmos, spanning more than a third of the sky, in 2031. Thursday’s release encompassed around 13 months of Euclid observations, totalling an enormous 1.7 petabytes 1.7 million gigabytes of data. “It marks a major milestone for ESA’s Euclid mission and for everyone involved,” said astrophysicist Valeria Pettorino, ESA’s Euclid project scientist. Euclid, launched from Florida in 2023, is gathering data on how the universe has expanded and how its structure has formed over time while amassing information about the nature of dark energy and dark matter and the role of gravity on large scales. “Euclid will not just take images of galaxies in the sky, in two dimensions, but will also measure their distance, the third dimension. This will tell us where galaxies are in space and time, across 10 billion years, and in all directions beyond our galactic plane,” Pettorino said. “Galaxies cluster along filaments, surrounded by empty space, and form a network that we call the cosmic web. Euclid will reconstruct the cosmic web and how it has grown over time. This is important because the exact configuration of the cosmic web, how many clusters or voids are there, how fast it changed, depend on the properties of dark energy and dark matter,” Pettorino said. The universe’s contents include ordinary matter as well as dark matter and dark energy. Ordinary matter stars, planets, gas, dust and all the familiar stuff on Earth represents about 5pc of the contents. Dark matter, known from the gravitational effects it exerts on galactic scales, is invisible material that may make up about 27pc of the cosmos. Dark energy, thought to be responsible for the accelerated expansion of the universe, may account for 68pc. Dark matter and dark energy do not emit or absorb light and cannot be directly observed. Gravitational lensing Previous Euclid data releases covered only a few days of observations. The newly released dataset includes more than a year of data and still spans only 14pc of the total sky area Euclid is due to survey in visible and near-infrared light over six years. This data release will be completed next year with the first results on dark energy and dark matter. Light travelling toward Earth from faraway galaxies can be bent and distorted by normal matter and dark matter in the foreground, an effect called gravitational lensing. Thus, the nearer galaxy’s gravity warps the light coming from the one behind. Published in Dawn, November 13th, 2026

items.title: OECD report reveals migration to developed countries is dwindling
items.description: PARIS: Migration to developed countries dwindled for a second year in a row in 2025, down 1.6pc compared to the previous year, according to an OECD report published on Thursday. While still experiencing high numbers, the 38 Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries recorded 6.1 million new permanent immigrants in 2025, compared to 6.2m the previous year. There has been a backlash in many Western countries against the arrival of irregular migrants fleeing conflict, authoritarian rule and economic hardship in their home countries. Legal humanitarian migration dropped “sharply” by 26pc in 2025 compared with 2024, the report found. Labour migration increased by 13pc. Permanent migration fell 14pc in US, 19pc in Canada and 32pc in UK last year While 2025 marked an overall decline in migration, the number of permanent immigrants settling for the long term was up 12pc compared with 2019. Three countries recorded a notable spike in permanent migrants in 2025. Portugal saw a 139pc increase to 313,600 individuals, resulting from approvals of a backlog of pending residency permits. Spain saw a 25pc increase to 460,500 people, notably after having broadened its residency policies. Italy saw a 45pc increase to 248,800 people, largely attributed to a flux of family and labour migration. Other countries saw significant declines in permanent migrants. The United States saw a 14pc drop, although it still leads OECD countries, recording more than 1.2m permanent migrants in 2025. Canada saw a 19pc decrease to 393,800 people, and the United Kingdom a 32pc decline to 295,800 people. Asylum seekers down India remained the leading country of origin for migratory flows to the OECD in 2024, ahead of China and Colombia, according to the latest available figures. The 1.1m asylum applications in 2025 marked a 22pc decrease to OECD countries, excluding the United States, compared with the previous year, although remaining about 10pc higher than 2019 figures. Men continue to account for the majority of migratory flows to OECD countries. According to the latest available data from 2024, women accounted for about 46pc of new immigrants. The OECD countries that admitted significantly more women than men were the United States and Ireland with 54pc female immigrants, Sweden with 53pc, and Israel, Chile, Australia and New Zealand with 52pc. Migration poses an opportunity to boost long-term productivity in many countries, particularly in the face of ageing populations, the OECD noted. “With the OECD working-age population set to decrease by 8pc by 2060, pushing overall growth downwards, reviving productivity growth is key to maintaining living standards,” said Mark Pearson, the OECD’s acting director of Employment, Labour and Social Affairs. Published in Dawn, November 13th, 2026

items.title: Gov’t plans 3% discount on GoldBod’s gold purchases after taking over programme costs from BoG
items.description: The government plans to introduce a 3% discount on small-scale gold purchases in 2027 to reduce the cost of accumulating foreign exchange and building reserves through domestic gold purchases. The measure, outlined in the 2027 Budget, comes after the transfer of the gold-buying programme from the Bank of Ghana to GoldBod, with the Ministry of Finance now responsible for financing its costs. According to the budget, the cost of generating foreign exchange through the Ghana Accelerated National Reserve Accumulation Policy fell from 16% in 2025 to 5% in 2026. Government now intends to reduce it further to 2%. “To reduce this cost further to 2 per cent, Government will, in consultation with industry stakeholders, introduce a 3 per cent discount on small-scale gold purchases in 2027,” the budget states. Finance Minister Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson The proposal addresses an important question raised by the programme’s earlier trading model: whether the price paid for gold leaves enough room to cover export costs and generate foreign exchange. Under the previous arrangement, GoldBod facilitated gold purchases on behalf of the Bank of Ghana, buying from small-scale miners at spot prices and, in some cases, at a premium. GoldBod earned fees for its services, while the central bank financed the purchases and absorbed the associated losses. The Bank of Ghana’s 2025 financial statements reported that the Domestic Gold Purchase Programme generated losses of approximately GH¢22 billion. BoG Governor, Dr Johnson Asiama JoyNews Research subsequently identified several sources of the losses, including service and assay fees, discounts on gold sold to off-takers and exchange-rate differences. Its analysis highlighted the gap between the forex bureau rate used to purchase gold and the reference rate used in the central bank’s accounting. Some losses reflected valuation effects rather than direct economic costs, but they nevertheless weakened the Bank of Ghana’s balance sheet. Responsibility for the programme has since changed. According to the government, GoldBod began conducting doré gold purchases on April 1, 2026. A memorandum signed in July formalised the transfer of the programme from the Bank of Ghana. GoldBod CEO, Sammy Gyamfi In practical terms, the transfer moved the financial burden away from the central bank. It did not automatically make the underlying transactions cheaper. The proposed discount now targets the purchase price itself. Buying gold at a lower price could create more room to cover refining, transport, financing and other trading costs. It could also reduce the amount government needs to provide to support the programme. The government’s own target suggests the discount will reduce the programme’s cost rather than eliminate it. Even after the proposed adjustment, the budget envisages a remaining cost of 2%. The government also has to balance reducing acquisition costs with keeping the official buying system attractive to miners and traders. A lower purchase price could improve the programme’s finances. But its effect on the volume of gold supplied through licensed channels will depend on the prices and payment terms available elsewhere. The budget says the government will develop the measure in consultation with industry stakeholders and specifically calls on the Ghana National Association of Small-Scale Miners and the Licensed Gold Buyers Associations to support the reforms. Government continues to emphasise the programme’s wider benefits. The budget reports that GoldBod has exported 88 tonnes of small-scale gold worth $12 billion since January 2026, supporting foreign-exchange supply, reserve accumulation and the cedi. Those benefits explain why the programme remains important to government. They also make it necessary to report its costs transparently. The 3% discount is a concrete response to the acquisition-cost problem. But transferring responsibility for financing the programme from the Bank of Ghana to the Ministry of Finance does not, in itself, resolve the underlying economics of the transactions. The proposed discount seeks to narrow that gap.

items.title: Peasant agriculture cannot solve Ghana’s food problems – Ato Forson
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson says Ghana must move beyond peasant agriculture and modernise food production to reduce its dependence on imports. Speaking in an interview on Thursday after presenting the 2027 Budget to Parliament, he argued that the country’s land, water resources and youthful population provided a strong foundation for commercial agriculture. “The current agriculture, peasant agriculture, cannot solve the problems.” Dr Forson said Ghana spends about US$3.5 billion annually importing foodstuffs. He described that level of dependence as unsustainable. “We spend about 3.5 billion United States dollars yearly to bring foodstuffs into our country. It cannot continue.” He responded to questions about proposed investment in commercial agriculture and agribusiness, including oil palm, sugar, rice, poultry, maize, soybean, aquaculture, vegetables, and cocoa. The minister questioned why Ghana kept importing products it could produce locally. He cited chicken imports of about US$200 million a year and called for stronger links between crop production and poultry farming. “Why can’t we use our land to grow soybean and maize to feed the poultry industry?” He also expressed concern about fish imports and Burkina Faso’s role in supplying onions and tomatoes. He identified Pwalugu as a potential part of the solution to vegetable supply challenges. “All we need to do is modernise agriculture.” Beyond food production, Dr Forson outlined plans to increase local cocoa processing rather than continue exporting beans for value addition elsewhere. He said the government wanted companies buying Ghanaian cocoa to establish processing operations in the country. “We are not saying don’t come and buy our cocoa beans, but if you are a company out there, come and buy our cocoa beans, but add value here in Ghana.” Asked about targets to process 50% of cocoa locally by 2028 and 100% by 2030, he said the new Cocoa Board Act already made the 50% requirement mandatory. He added that a legislative instrument would set the timeline for moving to full local processing by 2030. On processing capacity, Dr Forson said discussions were underway on a proposed contract involving 500,000 metric tonnes of cocoa for local value addition. He identified Dangote as the interested investor but said the terms were still being examined. “Dangote has reached out to use Ghana as a hub to process cocoa locally.”

items.title: France: Sweeping Bill Threatens Peaceful Protest, Rights
items.description: Click to expand Image Protesters gather in Place de la Nation square during a demonstration called by high-school students, joined by unions and teachers, who have been demanding better learning conditions, in Paris, France, on October 6, 2026. © 2026 Dimitar DILKOFF / AFP via Getty Images (Paris, November 12, 2026) – A draft law that passed in its first reading by the French Senate on October 27, 2026, contains measures that would severely undermine the rights to peaceful assembly and freedom of expression, and are incompatible with France’s human rights treaty obligations, Human Rights Watch said today. The so-called “vandals pay” bill is now pending review by the National Assembly. “Penalizing people engaged in their right to peaceful protest is the wrong answer to tackling violent disorder in France,” said Eva Cossé, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Lawmakers in both houses should reject this problematic bill entirely.” The bill was introduced by the government on September 16 under a fast-track procedure. It was pushed forward and significantly toughened by opposition conservative senators in response to weeks of nationwide high school protests over what students see as the government’s under-investment in their education, and the violence that took place alongside school and cost-of-living protests on October 17 that included significant clashes with law enforcement and widespread looting and property damage across France. The bill builds on the momentum of legislation adopted in August to address serious public disorder, developed in response to concerns over illegal dance parties, football-related rioting, and racing vehicles on the streets. While the purpose of the current legislation is ostensibly to address and deter violence and property damage, the text adopted by the Senate introduces measures that pose a serious threat to human rights, including the essence of the right to peaceful protest, Human Rights Watch said. The French authorities have also failed to put forward evidence that existing criminal justice measures are insufficient to address violent disorder or criminal damage. The draft law provides for joint civil liability for property damage during a protest. It would allow courts to order individual participants, including the parents of children who participated, to pay up to €10,000 in damages—or perform community service—whether or not the individual committed acts of violence or caused the damage. People could be penalized simply for “knowingly” participating in an “unlawful assembly” (attroupement), defined in the French criminal code as “any gathering of people on a public highway or in a public place that is likely to disturb public order,” or for failing to disperse after the police issue orders for a second time. Legal commentators have said that the requirement for prior dispersal orders is not an ineffective safeguard, because such orders are in practice either not issued or are not sufficiently audible. Being present during a protest considered an unlawful assembly, or failing to leave the area fast enough following police orders to disperse, could trigger severe financial consequences. The bill requires prosecutors to share suspects’ identities with prefects, the interior minister’s local representative, and local authorities so they can pursue damage claims in civil court, even if the prosecutor has decided not to pursue criminal charges. The bill would allow criminal penalties of up to one year in prison and a €15,000 fine for organizers of banned protests, and six months in prison and a €7,500 fine for participants, or in some cases, a summary fine of €500 to avoid prosecution. Existing law allows six months in prison and a €7,500 fine only for protest organizers. Punishments can be doubled for people who cover their faces. The bill also gives prefects the power, without prior judicial oversight, to preemptively ban individuals from protests for 24 hours on the basis of police intelligence or evidence of repeated or serious violent behavior during the three preceding years. The bill broadens existing security and administrative measures that jeopardize rights, Human Rights Watch said. To recover court-ordered damages, after a conviction, the draft law allows the state to confiscate social security payments—child benefit, early-years child allowance, family supplement, family support allowance, back-to-school allowance, and solidarity allocation—from parents to pay for damages caused by their children under age 18. This measure risks disproportionally affecting low-income households. It would also allow the authorities to deny social housing to adults convicted of “unlawful assembly” or serious public order offenses near residential buildings in the preceding three years, and to seek to evict families from social housing if a member of the household repeatedly engages in such acts. The bill broadens existing powers under counterterrorism, child protection, and drug laws, that oblige tech companies, without a court order, to take down within 24 hours online content that authorities deem capable of provoking offenses, under the threat of blocking the site and massive fines. The draft law extends the use of video surveillance to monitor public gatherings, and permits algorithmic processing to potentially identify protesters, measures first introduced for the Paris 2024 Olympics. Senators added a new provision to authorize recording and transmitting footage from drones and other police aircraft to track, identify, and prosecute individuals for protest-related offenses, raising the prospect of general drone surveillance by police. Previous laws imposed stricter conditions on police drone deployments to monitor protests. This draft law is part of a broader trend of erosion of the civic space and the rule of law in France, Human Rights Watch said. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights, to which France is a party, protect the rights to peaceful assembly and association and to freedom of expression. Although the treaties allow for restrictions on these rights, they must be subject to strict tests of necessity and proportionality. In particular, the European Court of Human Rights has consistently emphasized that peaceful participants in a protest may not be held responsible for reprehensible acts committed by others, and that “this is true even when the demonstration results in damage or other disorder.” The court has previously found France violated this standard, ruling that even a lower end disciplinary sanction imposed on a protester who did not commit any culpable act, was not permitted. The court reminded France that in seeking to pursue a legitimate aim, the result must not to be to discourage people, for fear of sanctions, from being able to express their views including through peaceful protest. Punishing individuals for the actions of others, and jailing and fining people simply for engaging in peaceful protest as a means of deterring violent disorder are not legitimate restrictions on those rights. The other measures in the bill also raise human rights concerns including in relation to the right to a fair trial, the right to privacy, and the rights to social security and housing. “This bill is a human rights disaster,” Cossé said. “It undermines human rights that are central to a functioning democracy, punishes people for the actions of others and not only risks, but seems designed to deter, participation in peaceful protest.”

items.title: Two arrested after pet lioness kills farmhouse worker in Lahore's Kahna
items.description: LAHORE: A farmhouse owner and a TikToker were arrested on Thursday after a 19-year-old farmhouse employee was killed by a pet lioness in the farmhouse in the Kahna area on Thursday. A spokesperson for the office of the deputy inspector general (DIG) of police identified the arrested suspects as farmhouse owner Fayyaz and TikToker Nauman. The spokesperson said Nauman had visited the farmhouse to make a TikTok video when the lioness allegedly went out of control and attacked Talha, a farm employee, leaving him critically injured. Talha was shifted to a private hospital where he died during treatment. Police investigations revealed that an attempt had allegedly been made to conceal the circumstances of the incident by describing it as a dog attack. However, an inquiry established that the victim had been attacked by a lioness. The animal was confiscated by the wildlife department while the victim’s body was shifted to a morgue for postmortem. A case was registered against the suspects. Police are also investigating whether the farmhouse had a valid permit to keep the lioness and had taken safety arrangements. DIG Operations Faisal Kamran said an attempt to conceal the facts and all aspects of possible negligence would be investigated. He said human life could not be put at risk in the name of entertainment or personal interests, adding that making TikTok videos could not take precedence over human life. Published in Dawn, November 13th, 2026

The exercise, held on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, marks the second time this year the MP has participated in the initiative to provide financial and other forms of assistance to persons with disabilities. The intervention supports efforts to promote social inclusion, improve the livelihoods of PWDs, and empower beneficiaries to become more economically independent. Mr Nokoe said the initiative reflects the government’s commitment, under President John Dramani Mahama’s leadership, to building an inclusive society where persons with disabilities have equal opportunities to participate in national development. He reaffirmed his commitment to supporting initiatives that improve the welfare of vulnerable groups, stressing the importance of ensuring that no one is left behind in the country’s development agenda.

items.title: 2027 Budget: Promised 24-hour economy incentives still missing
items.description: The 2027 Budget does not specify several incentives proposed to attract businesses into Ghana’s 24-hour economy programme; instead, it outlines a narrower set of tax measures for participating enterprises. The omissions include corporate income-tax rebates for businesses operating multiple shifts, discounted electricity tariffs for night-time production and rebates on manufactured exports. These were central features of the 283-page policy document released in July 2025 to support the NDC’s “1-3-3” vision of three people working successive eight-hour shifts in the same role. Source: 24-hour economy policy document The policy sought to make longer operating hours commercially attractive by reducing production costs and supporting business expansion. It proposed the following incentives: Corporate income-tax rebates: A 25% rebate for businesses operating two shifts and a 50% rebate for those running three shifts. Full corporate income-tax exemptions: For businesses in designated agricultural sectors, including grains, vegetables, oilseeds, tubers, livestock and sugar. Discounted night-time electricity: Reduced tariffs for businesses operating between 10 pm and 6 am. Import-duty exemptions on production inputs: Covering manufacturing equipment, raw materials and logistics infrastructure. Import-duty exemptions on renewable energy systems Targeted VAT exemptions: To help lower the cost of locally manufactured goods. Export rebates: Payments equivalent to 2%-6% of the value of manufactured exports. Quicker access to water and electricity for participating businesses. Priority regulatory clearance Long-term, low-interest loans: Financing through Development Bank Ghana Easier access to cocoa beans: For local cocoa processors enrolled in the programme. Alongside these incentives, the blueprint proposed large regional industrial parks known as Wumbei Parks. It also outlined plans for agricultural production and processing zones along the Volta Basin, supported by irrigation from the Volta Lake. The objective was to connect production, infrastructure and logistics to support continuous economic activity. However, the 2027 Budget and its accompanying presentation do not reproduce this incentive package. Instead, they identify three specific tax measures. The first is a deferral of import duty, levies and VAT on qualifying machinery and inputs . Businesses would postpone payment for one year, then settle the taxes in full over the following two years. The second is accelerated depreciation , allowing businesses to deduct the full cost of a qualifying asset over two years for tax purposes. The third is an exemption from import duties and VAT for solar panels and batteries . The budget explicitly identifies this as part of the 24-hour economy incentives, although the measure also covers households and businesses generally. These measures offer support, but their benefits differ from those envisaged under several of the original proposals. For example, deferring import taxes gives a company more time to pay. It does not remove the liability, as an exemption would. Similarly, accelerated depreciation brings forward deductions when calculating taxable profits. It does not provide the same benefit as the proposed 25% or 50% corporate income-tax rebate linked to additional shifts. The budget presentation also sets conditions for accessing the deferral and accelerated depreciation measures. Participating enterprises would be required to sign Performance Agreements containing binding commitments on job creation, additional investment, tax compliance and adoption of the 1-3-3 shift system. Yet the budget does not specify the corporate tax rebates originally proposed for businesses operating additional shifts. It also does not set out the discounted electricity tariff for production between 10 pm and 6 am or the manufactured-export rebates. That leaves an important question: are the announced measures an initial phase of the original package, or has the government revised what participating businesses should expect? Presidential Adviser on the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme The distinction matters because the government continues to describe the programme as private sector-led. A manufacturer considering a third shift would need to weigh the additional wages, electricity consumption and financing costs against the revenue it expects to earn. Cheaper night-time electricity and corporate tax rebates could influence that calculation. A tax deferral could help the same business acquire machinery, but it would not necessarily address the recurring cost of operating that machinery overnight. The budget provides other support for the programme. It allocates ¢165 million to the 24-Hour Economy Secretariat and proposes that the Ghana Sovereign Wealth Fund, to be formed by merging MIIF and the Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund, become an equity partner in programme projects. Those commitments could support implementation and investment. They do not, however, clarify the status of the wider incentives outlined in the July 2025 policy document. The original programme was estimated to require $4 billion initially, including $300 million in government seed capital, with the balance expected from public-private partnerships. The policy document also proposed a 2.5% levy on selected imports that could be produced locally to help fund the programme. Delivering the incentives would therefore require decisions about both financing and revenue. Tax exemptions and rebates would reduce government revenue in the short term, while the government expects increased production and investment to generate wider economic benefits. The original document did not provide a detailed fiscal calculation showing how much the incentives would cost or how additional revenue would offset that cost. The absence of several incentives from the 2027 Budget does not establish that they have been cancelled. But it leaves their implementation timetable and relationship with the newly announced measures unclear. The government will need to explain which of the original benefits it still intends to implement, which have been revised and when participating businesses can access them. The policy asks companies to invest, employ more people and operate additional shifts. Those companies need certainty about the support on which those decisions are expected to depend.

items.title: Samira Bawumia champions solar-powered healthcare, clean cooking at COP31
items.description: Former Second Lady of Ghana, Hajia Samira Bawumia, has called for increased investment in solar-powered healthcare systems and clean cooking solutions, highlighting their importance in protecting women and children from the health effects of climate change. She made the call during two high-level engagements at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, where she advocated practical interventions to connect climate action with improved health outcomes. At the Africa Women and Youth Climate Centre (AFRYWOCC) High-Level Dialogue, held at the World Health Organization’s Health Pavilion, Mrs Bawumia advocated solar-powered healthcare facilities to improve maternal and newborn health across Africa. She highlighted the Safe Delivery Project under the Samira Empowerment and Humanitarian Projects (SEHP), which aims to improve access to essential maternal healthcare services, particularly for women in underserved communities. Her intervention focused on providing reliable energy for healthcare facilities so women can access safe childbirth services, including in areas where electricity supply remains a challenge. The Health Pavilion is part of the WHO’s programme at COP31, which brings together health stakeholders to advance climate-related health solutions. At the Marrakech Partnership Axis 5 Showcase on Delivering Climate-Health Action, she shifted attention to clean cooking, urging stakeholders to accelerate access to cleaner cooking technologies to reduce health risks affecting women and children. She argued that climate change extends beyond environmental degradation, with household air pollution and reliance on traditional cooking fuels posing major threats to public health, particularly for vulnerable groups. Mrs Bawumia stressed that innovative financing, clean energy solutions, and stronger partnerships are needed to turn climate commitments into interventions that protect lives and improve living conditions. “The climate crisis is a health crisis,” she stated, calling for practical action as the international community looks towards COP32. Her participation in the two engagements reflects her continued advocacy for the intersection of climate action, healthcare and women’s empowerment, with particular attention to solutions that respond to the needs of African communities. The Marrakech Partnership showcase was held on November 11 under the Global Climate Action Agenda’s human and social development axis.

items.title: Ghana urges inclusive AI development as One Million Coders registrations exceed 140,000
items.description: Ghana has called for artificial intelligence (AI), satellite connectivity and other emerging technologies to be designed around people’s needs, warning that technological advancement must not deepen existing inequalities or leave underserved communities behind. The Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, made the call during a panel discussion on emerging technologies at the ongoing International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Plenipotentiary Conference 2026 in Doha, Qatar. He used the experiences of four hypothetical Ghanaians to show how international decisions on technology and digital policy could shape access to healthcare, connectivity, and economic opportunities. Highlighting AI’s potential in healthcare, the Minister cited an AI-powered service that lets pregnant women seek emergency assistance through basic mobile phones without needing internet access. He said the service had registered more than 7,000 mothers and expectant mothers at a single hospital in Ghana, showing how accessible technology could improve maternal healthcare. On digital connectivity, Mr George argued that extending network coverage alone was not enough, insisting that access must also be affordable, reliable and useful to communities. He called for increased investment in digital infrastructure, skills development and locally relevant content, particularly to address the needs of communities with limited access to technology. The Minister also raised concerns about allocating and managing satellite spectrum and orbital resources, stressing that these limited resources must be accessed fairly. He cautioned against allowing countries or companies that launch satellites first to claim ownership or exclusive control over space resources. On artificial intelligence, he advocated responsible, accountable systems that recognise local languages, reflect the realities of different communities, and provide avenues for explanation and redress when automated decisions affect individuals. “The question is not whether AI will shape Africa, but whether Africa will help shape AI,” he said, calling for stronger cooperation among governments, technology companies, academia and civil society to develop policies and standards that can work across national borders. Mr George also highlighted Ghana’s efforts to develop local technological expertise through the One Million Coders Programme, which has attracted more than 140,000 registrations. He said young people must be equipped not only to use emerging technologies but also to develop solutions, create innovations and participate meaningfully in the digital economy. The Minister further called for international partnerships that strengthen local capacity rather than create long-term dependence on external technologies. He identified technology transfer, increased investment, South-South cooperation, and the development of standards that address developing countries’ priorities as key areas for collaboration. He reaffirmed Ghana’s commitment to working with international partners to ensure emerging technologies advance digital inclusion, public trust and sustainable development.

items.title: ‘It cannot continue’ – Ato Forson challenges Ghana’s $3.5bn food import bill
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson has called for a shift towards modern commercial agriculture to reduce Ghana’s annual US$3.5 billion food import bill. Speaking in an interview on Thursday after presenting the 2027 Budget to Parliament, he said the country had the land, water resources and young population needed to produce more of its own food. “We spend about 3.5 billion United States dollars yearly to bring foodstuffs into our country. It cannot continue.” Dr Forson argued that the existing approach to farming could not meet the country’s needs. “The current agriculture, peasant agriculture, cannot solve the problems.” He questioned Ghana’s dependence on imported palm oil, sugar, rice and poultry. He said modernising agriculture could strengthen domestic production and supply industries that currently rely on imports. “Why should we be importing about $200 million of chicken every year?” he asked. He pointed to soybean and maize production as opportunities to support poultry farmers with locally produced feed. “Why can’t we use our land to grow soybean and maize to feed the poultry industry?” The minister also expressed concern about fish imports and Ghana’s reliance on neighbouring Burkina Faso for vegetables. “We spend hundreds of millions of dollars every year to bring in vegetables. Pwalugu can be the solution. Why can’t we do this?” Beyond food production, Dr Forson said Ghana must retain more value from its cocoa rather than continue exporting beans for processing elsewhere. He cited his experience in Bangkok, where he said he had seen a range of cocoa-based products. He argued that Ghana’s longstanding financing model encouraged buying and shipping beans instead of domestic processing. “We are not saying don’t come and buy our cocoa beans, but if you are a company out there, come and buy our cocoa beans, but add value here in Ghana.” Asked about targets to process 50% of Ghana’s cocoa locally by 2028 and 100% by 2030, Dr Forson said the new Cocoa Board Act already provided for the 50% requirement. He said a legislative instrument would set out the implementation timelines, including the move to full local processing by 2030. On processing capacity, the minister disclosed that Dangote had expressed interest in using Ghana as a cocoa-processing hub. He said discussions involved a proposed contract covering 500,000 metric tonnes of cocoa for local value addition. The terms were still being examined. “Dangote has reached out to use Ghana as a hub to process cocoa locally.”

items.title: ‘Do you want me to crash the country?’ – Ato Forson asks critics demanding huge spending
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson has defended the government’s expenditure record, saying a substantial part of available public funds is going towards settling inherited debts and restoring confidence in the economy rather than financing new spending. He said the government could not ignore its financial obligations and risk plunging the country into another economic crisis simply to satisfy demands for increased expenditure. Dr Forson disclosed that the government had so far paid GH¢41 billion to holders of bonds under the Domestic Debt Exchange Programme (DDEP), describing the payments as part of the difficult financial responsibilities inherited from the previous administration. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Thursday, November 12, after presenting the 2027 Budget to Parliament, he rejected criticism that he was not spending enough, insisting that the government was using available resources to meet pressing obligations. “I’m spending, but you see, people don’t appreciate it,” he said. “You see, I have this house that I have inherited from President Akufo-Addo’s government, and a large economic management team. These are debts that we have inherited. Do you want me to crash the country again? Do you? I can’t”. The Finance Minister said the government had inherited a difficult economic situation, including substantial debt obligations, which required careful management to prevent a return to financial instability. He said his immediate priority was to settle debts falling due, restore confidence in the market and move the country away from the economic crisis. “These are not normal times. I need to take the country off crisis. I need to restore market confidence. I need to pay the debt that has fallen due,” he said. Dr Forson explained that expenditure decisions had to be guided by the resources available to the government and the obligations it was required to meet. “I have my obligations. One, pay your debt; enough of what will be left, you will use it for others,” he said. He stressed that government could not spend money it did not have, arguing that responsible financial management required it to settle outstanding commitments before taking on additional expenditure. The GH¢41 billion figure cited by the minister is consistent with the Finance Ministry’s August 2026 disclosure that total payments to DDEP bondholders since 2025 had reached GH¢41.36 billion, following a GH¢10.8 billion coupon payment made on August 18, 2026. Debt payments and development spending The minister’s defence comes against the backdrop of the 2027 Budget, which projects total government expenditure of GH¢389.2 billion for the coming fiscal year. Of that amount, GH¢100.4 billion has been allocated to capital expenditure, while GH¢61 billion is earmarked for interest payments on domestic and external debt. The budget also provides GH¢104.1 billion for employee compensation and GH¢13.9 billion for the clearance of arrears. Dr Forson has also announced plans to settle GH¢29 billion in DDEP principal falling due in February 2027 ahead of schedule, following an early redemption offer to bondholders. Government further intends to pay a US$590 million Eurobond obligation due in January 2027 by December 31, 2026. Together, the two repayments are expected to clear more than GH¢36 billion in debt ahead of their maturity dates. The Finance Minister said the government’s approach was intended to prevent the country from returning to the financial difficulties that necessitated the debt restructuring. He maintained that the administration had to balance its development ambitions with the responsibility of meeting debt obligations and preserving the economic gains made so far.

items.title: IJM Ghana donates mattresses, appliances to support human trafficking survivors
items.description: The International Justice Mission (IJM) Ghana donated mattresses and household appliances to the Human Trafficking Female Adult Shelter, operated under the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, to improve living conditions for survivors receiving care at the facility. The items were presented by IJM Ghana Country Director and West Africa Programme Director, Anita Budu, who reaffirmed the organisation’s commitment to supporting the government’s efforts to protect victims of human trafficking. She said providing safe, well-equipped shelter facilities was essential to the recovery, rehabilitation, and eventual reintegration of survivors. Receiving the donation on behalf of the Ministry, Gender, Children and Social Protection Minister, Dr Agnes Naa Momo Lartey, expressed appreciation to IJM Ghana for its continued partnership and support. She said the items would address some of the shelter’s identified needs, improve residents’ comfort, and support the facility’s daily operations. Dr Lartey also acknowledged President John Dramani Mahama’s commitment to strengthening Ghana’s response to human trafficking and protecting survivors. The Minister said Ghana’s attainment of Tier 1 status in the 2026 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report reflected the combined efforts of government institutions, development partners and other stakeholders working to combat the crime. She stressed the need to sustain such partnerships to protect the country’s progress and strengthen support systems for survivors. Following an assessment of the shelter’s needs, the donation included 10 mattresses, a Midea gas cooker, a blender, a 43-inch Samsung television, and a Midea refrigerator, among other essential items. The Ministry expressed gratitude to IJM Ghana and its other development partners for contributing to efforts to ensure that survivors of human trafficking receive the protection, care and assistance needed to rebuild their lives.

items.title: Consumer courts can’t hear insurance policyholder's complaints, LHC holds
items.description: LAHORE: The Lahore High Court has ruled that consumer courts lack jurisdiction to entertain complaints filed by policyholders against insurance companies. Justice Jawad Hassan issued the ruling on a petition filed by the United Insurance Company of Pakistan Limited against an order passed by the District Consumer Court in Bhakkar. The consumer court had overruled an objection raised by the insurance firm regarding the maintainability of a complaint filed by a policyholder. The district court had held that the complaint was maintainable simply because the dispute stemmed from the provision of insurance services. Setting aside the consumer court’s order, Justice Hassan observed that the lower forum failed to properly examine the relevant statutory framework, specifically Section 122 of the Insurance Ordinance, 2000. The judge noted that Section 122(3) of the Ordinance explicitly bars any court other than a specialised tribunal from exercising jurisdiction over claims brought by a policyholder against an insurance company in respect of or arising out of an insurance policy. Orders issuance of fresh, reasoned decision on case’s maintainability within a month Referring to constitutional principles and settled judicial precedents, including the landmark Adamjee Insurance Company case, Justice Hassan highlighted that under Article 143 of the Constitution, competent federal legislation takes precedence over provincial enactments. Consequently, he said, where a special statute provides a specific mechanism and forum for dispute resolution, general laws such as consumer protection acts cannot be invoked to displace the jurisdiction of the specialised tribunal. The judge remanded the matter back to the consumer court with directions to re-examine the question of maintainability strictly in accordance with the law and binding judicial precedents. The judge said a fresh and reasoned decision should be issued within one month. Published in Dawn, November 13th, 2026

items.title: NDPC reviews national monitoring and evaluation manual to strengthen development planning
items.description: The National Development Planning Commission (NDPC) has begun a stakeholder review of the second edition of Ghana’s National Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) Manual to improve its effectiveness and application across public institutions. The exercise, held on Thursday, November 12, 2026, brought together representatives from government agencies, local authorities, development partners, academia, research institutions and civil society organisations to examine the draft document and propose amendments. Welcoming participants, NDPC Director-General, Dr Audrey Smock Amoah, said the revision was necessary to reflect changes in Ghana’s legal, institutional and development planning environment since the first edition was introduced in 2013. She explained that the updated manual was not intended to replace the existing national monitoring and evaluation framework but to improve how it operates and supports development planning. Dr Smock Amoah stressed that monitoring and evaluation should be incorporated into the design of policies, plans, programmes and projects, rather than treated as an activity undertaken after implementation. She added that evidence generated through the process must guide project implementation, budget decisions, policymaking and institutional accountability. The Director-General urged stakeholders to make practical contributions, particularly on institutional mandates, reporting procedures, monitoring tools and templates, and the feasibility of applying the guidelines at national and local levels.The Director of Monitoring and Evaluation at the NDPC, Bright Yaw Atiase, also urged participants to ensure their institutions’ recommendations were captured in the revised document. He emphasised that the manual was designed for use across the country’s development planning system and was not an internal guide for the NDPC alone. Mr Atiase identified incorporating knowledge management as a significant addition, explaining that strengthening the generation, sharing, and use of knowledge would improve policy formulation and management decisions. The stakeholder review is expected to produce consolidated recommendations, agreed changes to the draft, designated institutional focal persons and a timeline for completing the second edition. Participants included representatives of Ministries, Departments and Agencies, Regional Coordinating Councils, Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies, development partners, universities, research institutions, M&E professional bodies and civil society organisations.

En ese bloque la fuerza emergente es la extrema derecha frente a un PP estancado. De tal modo que las valoraciones ciudadanas del líder de Vox, Santiago Abascal, y del popular Alberto Núñez Feijóo están prácticamente igualadas. Antes de empezar, destacamos tres novelas notables que han llegado en las últimas semanas a las librerías, pero de las que nos hemos ocupado en capítulos aparte o en Babelia. Acebedo, ese misterioso pseudónimo detrás del que se esconde el autor de las novelas de Gonzalo de Berceo como pesquisidor. La última se titula Una tumba en Al Andalus (Tusquets) y tiene mucha sangre y mucha diversión, según la crítica de Manuel Morales , que acercó su afinado criterio a esta sección de ficción criminal. items.title: ¡Qué hijo de gran señora!
items.description: Enganché por puro azar a unos manifestantes que eran el grupo perfecto para un estudio de mercado. Llevaban una de las pocas pancartas escritas sobre lona que resistía la lluvia. “Lavapiés con la Huelga General 11-N”. Eran treintañeros y no portaban ningún otro símbolo distintivo político o sindical. Caminé junto a ellos durante algo más de una hora, escuchando sus lemas, mezcla de ingenio y rabia generacional. A menudo, tiraban de ironía: “Queremos donut sin agujerito, vinos sin sulfitos y comprarnos un pisito”. De tanto en tanto, un cántico tradicional boomer se cruzaba bajo los paraguas. “¡De norte a sur, de este a oeste, la huelga sigue, cueste lo que cueste!”. El grupo lo coreaba solidario, pero en cuanto la voz se perdía entre el bosque de varillas retomaban su tono mezcla de kawaii , “Queremos un pisito como el del principito”, y dureza reivindicativa: “No queremos hacer las paces, esto es la lucha de clases”. items.title: De la ‘Kiss Cam’ al CEO de Nvidia: la lista de altos ejecutivos que perdieron el cargo por un amor prohibido
items.description: Las relaciones sentimentales secretas no caben en la cultura empresarial de Estados Unidos. En la mayoría de los supuestos, incluso está prohibido por contrato no solo entre un superior y un empleado, sino entre los propios trabajadores. El caso de Jensen Huang, máximo responsable de Nvidia, que ha sido la mayor empresa del mundo por capitalización hasta hace unos días, ha sido doble. Y parece trascender lo personal, como ha sucedido con el primero de los escándalos conocidos, el que lo vinculó a Alice Huang , a quien se le señala como supuesta espía industrial para China. Seguir leyendo Harry Stonecipher (Boeing, 2005) El fabricante aeronáutico estadounidense Boeing obligó a dimitir a su presidente y consejero delegado Harry Stonecipher, tras ser investigado por su relación con una directiva del grupo. La compañía abrió una investigación interna tras recibir una denuncia anónima. El presidente de la junta, Lew Platt, explicó que la investigación determinó que Stonecipher había violado el código de conducta de Boeing. La ejecutiva, cuya identidad no fue revelada, no se encontraba bajo órdenes directas de Stonecipher y su estatus en la empresa no se vio afectado. Platt señaló que "los hechos reflejan un mal criterio por parte del ejecutivo (casado y de 68 años de edad) que perjudica su capacidad para liderar la compañía". Mark Hurd (HP, 2010) Mark Hurd, uno de los ejecutivos más admirados dentro y fuera del sector tecnológico, dimitió por sorpresa, envuelto en un escándalo sexual. El consejero delegado de Hewlett Packard (HP) de 2005 a 2010 mantuvo durante año y medio una relación secreta con una contratista de la compañía, con la que no escatimó en gastos, como cenas íntimas por todo el mundo, que cargó a la empresa. A raíz de una denuncia por acoso sexual, la compañía inició una investigación interna. Sin embargo, en el comunicado de la compañía que explicaba los motivos de la salida de Hurd, el consejo de administración de HP dejó claro que no se detectó ninguna violación de la llamada política antiacoso, aunque sí de su código de conducta. Brian Krzanich (Intel, 2018) El director ejecutivo de Intel, Brian Krzanich, dimitió en junio de 2019 tras conocerse la relación que mantuvo con una empleada . La compañía, uno de los mayores fabricantes de chips del mundo, afirmó que dicha relación violaba su código de conducta. En un comunicado, explicó: "Una investigación en curso, realizada por asesores legales internos y externos, ha confirmado una infracción de la política de Intel que prohíbe las relaciones personales en el lugar de trabajo, aplicable a todos los directivos. Dada la expectativa de que todos los empleados respeten los valores de la compañía y se adhieran a su código de conducta, la junta directiva ha aceptado la renuncia del Sr. Krzanich". Steve Easterbrook (McDonald's, 2019) El consejo de McDonald’s despidió a su primer ejecutivo, Steve Easterbrook, en 2019 por falta de juicio y por mantener una relación personal inapropiada con una empleada de la compañía, lo que infringía la política de la empresa. Pero no era la única. El directivo británico ocultó que había tenido relaciones sexuales con más trabajadoras de la empresa para mantener su alta indemnización. Mintió cuando le preguntaron expresamente por ello y le salió caro. Tuvo que devolver primero la multimillonaria compensación y luego tuvo que pagar una multa a la Comisión de Bolsa y Valores estadounidense (la SEC) por sus mentiras. Mark Wiseman (BlackRock, 2019) Cuando en diciembre de 2019 Mark Wiseman postulaba a heredar el máximo cargo de BlackRock, fue despedido por no revelar una relación inapropiada dentro de la empresa. “Tuve una relación consensuada con una de nuestras colegas sin informarlo”, declaró Wiseman. “Lamento mi error y acepto la responsabilidad de mis actos”. El fondo de inversión exige a sus empleados que revelen a la empresa cualquier relación. Por otro lado, Wiseman estaba casado con otra ejecutiva de BlackRock. Jeff Zucker (CNN, 2022) El presidente de la icónica cadena de televisión CNN, Jeff Zucker, anunció en febrero de 2022 la renuncia a su cargo por una relación dentro de la compañía. "Como parte de la investigación interna, me preguntaron sobre una relación consensuada con mi colega más cercana, alguien con quien he trabajado durante más de 20 años", declaró Zucker a los empleados en un memorando interno. "Reconocí que la relación evolucionó en los últimos años. Se me exigió que lo revelara cuando comenzó, pero no lo hice. Me equivoque. Por lo tanto, renuncio hoy". Bernard Looney (BP, 2023) El consejero delegado de la petrolera británica BP, Bernard Looney, notificó su dimisión tras admitir que no fue "completamente transparente" al informar sobre las "relaciones personales" que mantuvo con colegas de la empresa. Looney, de 53 años, se unió a la compañía en 1991 y fue designado consejero delegado en 2020 con el objetivo de liderar la firma en un entorno de transición energetica. Según comunicó la compañía, el consejo de administración recibió y analizó en mayo de 2022 acusaciones anónimas sobre la "conducta" de Looney "en sus relaciones personales con colegas de la compañía". Andy Byron (Astronomer, 2025) El primer ejecutivo de Astronomer, Andy Byron, renunció a su cargo tras hacerse viral un vídeo en el que aparecía abrazando a una mujer que no era su esposa e identificada como la jefa de recursos humanos de la misma empresa, Kristin Cabot, durante un concierto de Coldplay en Boston el pasado 16 de julio. La compañía especializada en herramientas de orquestación de datos para empresas decidió abrir "una investigación formal" tras difundirse masivamente el vídeo. En la red social X, la empresa señaló que se guía "por ciertos valores" y que de sus directivos "espera que cumplan los requisitos tanto de conducta como de rendición de cuentas". Laurent Freixe (Nestlé, 2025) El consejo de administración de Nestlé, la mayor empresa de alimentación de toda Europa, comunicó el 1 de septiembre de 2025 el cese inmediato de su consejero delegado, Laurent Freixe, tras una investigación sobre una “relación romántica no declarada con una subordinada directa“ que mantenía. La firma explicó que la relación sentimental que el destituido consejero delegado mantenía en secreto contraviene el código de conducta de la multinacional suiza. Freixe había sido nombrado máximo ejecutivo de la compañía en el verano de 2024, pero llevaba en la empresa desde el añpo 1986.

Al transcribir una de las grabaciones, la Unidad de Asuntos Internos (UAI) puso como “ininteligible” un pasaje donde la exdirigente del PP pregunta “quién tiene lo de Aznar”. El PSOE, personado como acusación popular, ya ha solicitado a la Audiencia Nacional que corrija esa parte del informe sobre el audio, cuyo original se escucha muy bajo y que EL PAÍS ha ampliado para comprobar su contenido. Los socialistas consideran importante incluir esa mención expresa para entender la trama, mientras se mantienen a la espera de que la Audiencia Nacional decida si retoma las pesquisas contra Cospedal. items.title: El ático que el Gobierno de Ayuso adquirió por 6,3 millones se queda en un limbo: ni se usa, ni se vende
items.description: El ático adquirido por el gobierno de Isabel Díaz Ayuso (PP) en la Comunidad de Madrid se ha quedado en un limbo desde que en julio EL PAÍS desveló su compra . Planifica Madrid, una empresa pública, lo había incorporado en abril a su cartera por 6,3 millones de euros. Un día después de conocerse públicamente la operación, la Comunidad decidió venderlo por 6,7 millones , con la excusa de dedicar la recaudación a paliar los efectos del fuego en la Sierra Oeste. Casi cuatro meses después, nada ha ocurrido: el ático no se usa, ni se vende. La subasta correspondiente ha quedado desierta dos veces . Tampoco ha llegado ninguna oferta durante el proceso permanente de venta abierto tras esos fiascos, cuyo primer plazo venció sin éxito el lunes, por lo que fue extendido hasta el 24 de noviembre. Expertos consultados por este diario señalan como explicación una mezcla de desincentivos: el precio puede ser alto, pues supera los siete millones con impuestos; no hay opción de negociarlo a la baja; y el comprador sabe que se expone al coste reputacional de ser examinado con lupa por la oposición y los medios. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Condenada al atasco: el transporte público de Valencia no crece al ritmo que la población metropolitana
items.description: El transporte público está viviendo una revolución enorme. De 2019 a 2025, que es cuando hay datos disponibles, Metrovalencia ha incrementado más de un 30% sus viajeros, la EMT más de un 25%, las Cercanías de Renfe ha aumentado también después de años de descensos. Y Metrobús, los autobuses metropolitanos, casi han duplicado los viajeros en esos seis años. “¿Qué ocurre?“, plantea Tomás Ruiz desde la Cátedra de Transportes y Sociedad de la Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV), cuyo equipo ha elaborado un estudio reciente sobre la movilidad en Valencia y su área metropolitana. Que la dependencia del coche privado continúa en los viajes entre el área metropolitana y la capital debido a una insuficiente oferta de transporte colectivo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: African Political Parties Initiative announces inaugural leadership, with Asiedu Nketiah as chair
items.description: Ghana’s National Democratic Congress (NDC) National Chairman, Johnson Asiedu Nketiah, has been named the inaugural Chair of the African Political Parties Initiative (APPI), placing him at the head of a continental platform seeking to strengthen political party institutions and cooperation across Africa. The African Governance Centre (AGC), which established the initiative, announced the composition of APPI’s inaugural Bureau Leadership following the Second African Political Parties Summit (APPS 2026), held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, from November 5 to 7. Mr Asiedu Nketiah was endorsed as Chair on November 7, following his nomination by an interim committee and approval by participating political parties at the summit. The Bureau will serve an initial three-year term. The Bureau is supported by ten Regional Vice-Chairs representing political parties across Africa’s five regions. In North Africa , the representatives are Prof. Benmebarek Abdelkrim of Algeria’s Front de Libération Nationale (FLN) and H.E. Dr Mohamed Ould Mouloud, President of Mauritania’s Union of Forces of Progress. West Africa is represented by Dr Luther Tarpeh, Chairman of Liberia’s Unity Party, and H.E. Pascal Affi N’Guessan, President of Côte d’Ivoire’s Front Populaire Ivoirien and a former Prime Minister. For Central Africa , the appointees are Hon. Augustin Kabuya Tshilumba, President and Secretary-General of the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS), and Hon. Joshua Osih, Chairman of Cameroon’s Social Democratic Front (SDF). East Africa has Dr Asha-Rose Migiro, Secretary-General of Tanzania’s Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM), and Rt. Hon. Richard Todwong, Secretary-General of Uganda’s National Resistance Movement (NRM). The two representatives for Southern Africa are Hon. Nthatii Moorosi, Secretary-General of Lesotho’s Revolution for Prosperity, and Hon. Sophia Shaningwa, Secretary-General of Namibia’s SWAPO Party. The Bureau also includes representatives responsible for the initiative’s institutional and programme activities. Benedicta Lasi, Founder and Chair of the Africa Governance Centre, will serve as Institutional Co-Chair, while the Centre’s Executive Director, Prof. Nelson Oppong, joins as an Institutional Member. Dr Bikila Hurisa of Ethiopia’s Prosperity Party has been appointed Executive Secretary of APPI. Other appointments include Prof. Modeste Bahati Lukwebo of the Democratic Republic of Congo, who will chair the Council of African Political Party Schools and Institutes (CAPPSI). Yvonne Aki-Sawyerr, Mayor of Freetown in Sierra Leone, will chair the African Women Political Leadership Summit (AWPLS), while Dr Abdullahi Dayo Israel of Nigeria will lead the African Youth Political Forum (AYPF). During its initial three-year term, the Bureau is expected to guide APPI’s membership and procedural arrangements, strengthen cooperation among participating political parties, and advance political education and leadership development across the continent. A major priority will be consultations on APPI Agenda 2040, a proposed long-term framework aimed at strengthening political party institutions, policy capacity and their contribution to Africa’s development. The initiative is also expected to promote the development of party schools, policy institutes and research institutions, as well as encourage greater participation by women and young people in political decision-making. In his acceptance address on November 7, Mr Asiedu Nketiah called on political parties to look beyond electoral victories and invest in the structures, expertise and policy knowledge needed to govern effectively. APPI was formally launched in Accra in March 2025 under the auspices of the Africa Governance Centre. Its first African Political Parties Summit was subsequently held in Accra from August 12 to 14, 2025, bringing together political leaders and governance stakeholders from across the continent. The second summit was held in Addis Ababa in partnership with Ethiopia’s ruling Prosperity Party under the theme, “Governing for Growth: African Political Parties as Architects of Africa’s Economic Future”. The gathering concluded with the adoption of the Addis Ababa Declaration, which outlines a framework for strengthening political leadership, democratic governance and the role of political parties in Africa’s economic transformation. The Africa Governance Centre has congratulated the inaugural Bureau members and pledged to work with the leadership to advance APPI’s objectives.

items.title: Mahama discusses lecturers’ welfare, university funding with UTAG
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has engaged the leadership of the University Teachers Association of Ghana (UTAG) on a range of concerns, including lecturers’ welfare, recruitment challenges, research funding and tensions with the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC). The discussions took place at the Presidency on Thursday, November 12, 2026, when a delegation led by UTAG President, Professor Vera Ogeh Fiador, met the President to present issues affecting university teachers and the wider tertiary education sector. The association raised concerns about the proposed National Research Fund, the Book and Research Allowance, the retirement age of university lecturers, recruitment and emoluments, as well as its demand for the removal of the GTEC Director-General. UTAG also pushed for import duty exemptions on vehicles and research equipment owned by its members. The delegation further discussed the need for more student hostel facilities, illegal small-scale mining, the ongoing constitutional review process and the state of the economy. The Education Minister assured the lecturers that the government remained committed to safeguarding academic freedom, stressing that its priority was to provide the infrastructure and institutional support required to improve educational standards. He also updated the association on steps being taken to resolve its disagreement with the GTEC Director-General, indicating that an arbitration panel chaired by his Deputy, Dr Clement Apaak, was working towards settling the matter. On accommodation challenges in public universities, President Mahama disclosed the government’s intention to collaborate with private investors to construct student hostels on university campuses. He also addressed UTAG’s concerns about delays in recruitment, explaining that the tight compensation budget for public sector workers had made it necessary for the Finance Minister to exercise control over financial clearance for new appointments. The President, however, expressed confidence that continued economic growth following the country’s recovery would expand available resources, creating room to improve conditions of service and address outstanding demands. On the UTAG-GTEC dispute, he called for an amicable settlement, expressing the hope that both parties would reach a resolution to ease tensions within the tertiary education sector.

items.title: ‘Come and buy our cocoa beans, but add value here in Ghana’ – Forson
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson has urged international cocoa buyers to process beans in Ghana, as the government pursues plans to increase local processing to 50% by 2028 and 100% by 2030. Speaking in an interview on Thursday after presenting the 2027 Budget to Parliament, he said Ghana must move beyond exporting raw beans for other countries to process. “We are not saying don’t come and buy our cocoa beans, but if you are a company out there, come and buy our cocoa beans, but add value here in Ghana.” Dr Forson argued that Ghana’s longstanding financing model encouraged buying and shipping beans abroad, allowing other economies to capture the benefits of processing. He said a recent visit to Bangkok for the World Bank–IMF Annual Meetings reinforced his conviction about the opportunities in cocoa value addition. “I was shocked by what they’ve done with cocoa,” he said, citing products ranging from chocolate to cocoa cognac. Asked whether the government would use legislation to enforce local processing, the minister said the new Cocoa Board Act already included the requirement and had gone to Parliament. “It’s mandatory. Cocoa Board has to produce 50% of its cocoa locally, processing locally.” He said a Legislative Instrument would set out the timetable for reaching full local processing. “The LI that will back it will specify that by 2030, by 2030 move from 50 to 100 per cent.” Responding to questions about processing capacity, Dr Forson disclosed discussions over a proposed arrangement involving 500,000 metric tonnes of cocoa for local value addition. He said the terms were being reviewed and identified Dangote as the interested investor. “Dangote has reached out to use Ghana as a hub to process cocoa locally.” The cocoa plans form part of the minister’s broader argument for modernising agriculture and reducing dependence on imported food. Dr Forson said Ghana had land, water resources and a youthful population that could support a stronger agricultural sector. “The current agriculture, peasant agriculture, cannot solve the problems.” He put annual food imports at about US$3.5 billion and questioned why Ghana continued to import palm oil, sugar, rice, chicken and vegetables. “We spend about 3.5 billion United States dollars yearly to bring foodstuffs into our country. It cannot continue.” He also questioned why more land could not be used to grow soybean and maize to supply the poultry industry. For Dr Forson, investing in commercial agriculture and local processing offers a way to use Ghana’s resources better while keeping more value in the economy.
